analysis.one_liner: Lets shooting victims sue handgun and assault-weapon makers, importers, and dealers for damages without proving fault.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in January 1995, referred to the House Judiciary Committee's Crime Subcommittee, and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a new federal right to sue. Anyone shot with a handgun or assault weapon — or the family of someone killed — could sue the gun's manufacturer, importer, or dealer in federal court and win damages without proving the gun was defective or the seller did anything wrong. The gun industry would bear the cost of shootings involving its products, with exceptions for injuries to people committing felonies, self-inflicted wounds, and police or military shootings. It applied only to guns made, imported, or sold after the law took effect.
analysis.who_benefits: Victims of handgun and assault-weapon shootings and their families. They would gain a federal cause of action against the gun's maker, importer, or seller, would not have to prove fault or a defect, could collect direct and consequential damages, and could ask the court for attorney's fees [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Any person injured or killed by the discharge of a handgun or assault weapon could sue any manufacturer, importer, or dealer of that gun in U.S. district court.

Defendants would be strictly liable — responsible for all direct and consequential damages without any showing of fault or defect — except when the victim was committing a felony, was self-injured, or was shot by police or military personnel in the line of duty.
Courts could award reasonable attorney's fees to the prevailing party, and suits could be filed within two years of discovering the injury.

analysis.who_pays: Firearms manufacturers, importers, and dealers, who would be liable for damages from shootings involving guns they placed on the market after enactment, regardless of fault. Those costs would be borne directly through damage awards, legal fees, and liability insurance, and would likely be passed to gun buyers in higher prices.

drawbacks.text: Traditional products liability holds makers responsible for defective products; this bill would have held them financially responsible for the criminal or negligent misuse of lawful, non-defective products, a much broader form of liability.

Strict liability would expose the industry to damage claims for nearly every criminal shooting involving a covered gun, creating potentially open-ended costs that manufacturers and dealers would likely pass to consumers through higher prices or absorb by leaving parts of the market.
The bill offered compensation after shootings occurred; it contained no provisions to prevent gun violence in the first place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For victims, the bill offered a real remedy: money damages from deep-pocketed defendants without the usual burden of proving negligence or a defect, plus possible attorney's fees. The cost fell on the firearms industry and, through prices, on gun buyers. The core design — strict liability without fault — is a deliberate policy choice that most courts and legislatures reject for lawful products; supporters saw it as making the industry internalize the costs of gun violence, while critics saw it as punishing lawful commerce for crimes the industry does not commit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its Crime Subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Cardiss Collins introduced the bill on January 4, 1995, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
On January 25, 1995, it was referred to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on Crime, the last action ever taken on it.
The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in the House or Senate, and expired when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms manufacturers, importers, and dealers are better off: they never faced the strict-liability regime the bill would have imposed, and the bill's death preserved the existing legal rule that gun sellers are not liable for criminal misuse of their lawful products. Shooting victims gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Cardiss Collins
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it in the House.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on January 4, 1995, referred it to the Subcommittee on Crime, and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Subcommittee on Crime
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 25, 1995, and never held a hearing or vote on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democrats — the sponsor and one cosponsor — are on record in support, and no committee or floor vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of opposition never showed up in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have made them strictly liable for damages from shootings involving handguns and assault weapons they placed on the market, regardless of fault. Its death preserved their existing protection from such suits.
Strict liability for the gun industry would have meant a new, potentially enormous class of insured claims, and insurers would have priced that risk into gun-industry coverage.
